explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves row-count messages enabled in usp_TestProcedure, increasing network and client chatter.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF is specified in a procedure that uses explicit transactions, risking open or partially applied transactions after runtime errors.
SELECT * on Sales.Orders retrieves all columns unnecessarily and couples callers to schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) on Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY clause, returning an arbitrary set of rows.
DISTINCT is redundant when selecting OrderID, which is already the primary key of Sales.Orders.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders can read uncommitted data, skip rows, or read duplicate rows.
Applying YEAR() directly to o.OrderDate prevents sargable range filtering on Sales.Orders.
Comparing int column o.CustomerID to nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText forces an implicit type conversion.
Using (@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID) inhibits index seeks and causes poor plan reuse on Sales.Orders.
The leading wildcard pattern N'%urgent%' on o.Comments forces a full scan rather than an index seek.
Using NOT IN against a subquery on Sales.Invoices risks returning empty results if the subquery column can ever produce NULL; prefer NOT EXISTS.
Wrapping o.CustomerID in ISNULL() prevents the optimizer from seeking on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
Performing arithmetic (o.OrderID + 0) in the WHERE clause prevents a direct index seek on PK_Sales_Orders.
The inequality predicate o.CustomerID <> 1 is poorly selective and typically forces a broad scan.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join condition, producing a Cartesian product.
Comma-separated join syntax between Sales.Orders and Sales.OrderLines obscures join predicates; use explicit INNER JOIN.
The scalar subquery counting rows in Sales.OrderLines executes per outer row of Sales.Orders instead of using a set-based join/aggregate.
The correlated EXISTS subquery against Sales.OrderLines checks existence per row of Sales.Orders where a set operation could be used.
The CASE expression checking o.Comments IS NULL is duplicated in both the SELECT list and ORDER BY clause.
ORDER BY 2 relies on select-list ordinal position, which breaks easily if columns are reordered or added.
OFFSET ... FETCH orders only by non-unique o.OrderDate without a unique tie-breaker like o.OrderID, making pagination nondeterministic.
UNION between disjoint predicates (o.OrderID = 1 and o.OrderID = 2) adds unnecessary sort/deduplication overhead compared to UNION ALL.
Using (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines ...) > 0 counts all matching rows when EXISTS would stop at the first match.
Assigning @OrderID via SELECT from Sales.Orders without a unique filter silently overwrites the variable across multiple rows and keeps an arbitrary last value.
Declaring table variable @OrderIds can lead to fixed or poor cardinality estimates compared to a temporary table.
SELECT TOP (5) inserting into @OrderIds lacks an ORDER BY clause, selecting arbitrary rows from Sales.Orders.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders implicitly defines the temp table schema instead of using an explicit CREATE TABLE.
SELECT TOP (5) into #ImplicitOrders has no ORDER BY clause, populating the temp table with arbitrary rows.
order_cursor iterates over Sales.Orders row by row instead of using a set-based query.
The WHILE @Counter <= 1 loop performs procedural iteration rather than set-based processing.
Building @Sql by concatenating @CustomerID prevents query plan parameterization and complicates maintenance.
EXEC (@Sql) executes dynamic SQL without parameter binding.
Building @Sql by concatenating @OrderID embeds values directly into the SQL text instead of using parameter placeholders.
EXEC sys.sp_executesql @Sql is called without parameter definitions or bound values.
Temporary table #Scratch is created explicitly but never dropped before the procedure ends.
The CATCH block selects ERROR_MESSAGE() as a result set and swallows the exception without rethrowing via THROW.
RAISERROR is legacy error-raising syntax; prefer THROW for modern error handling.
PRINT outputs buffered diagnostic text that is unsuitable for production logging.
Hard-coding CustomerID = 1 embeds a magic business identifier directly in the query.
The date literal '20160101' is hard-coded directly into the filter on o.OrderDate without a named parameter or variable.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits an explicit style code and uses a locale-ambiguous date format.
Using COALESCE on o.CustomerID and i.CustomerID in the JOIN predicate prevents index seeks on the join columns.
SELECT TOP (1) in the join between Sales.Orders and Sales.Invoices has no ORDER BY clause.
Self-joining Sales.Orders to itself on OrderID retrieves no data that isn't already on the single row.
SELECT TOP (1) in the self-join on Sales.Orders specifies no ORDER BY clause.
Sorting Sales.Orders by o.Comments (nvarchar(max)) requires a high-memory sort over a wide LOB column.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire Sales.OrderLines table without any WHERE filter.
Filtering ol.OrderID > 0 in HAVING applies a non-aggregate row filter after grouping instead of in WHERE.
ORDER BY OrderCount on an ungrouped scalar COUNT(*) query is redundant because only one row is returned.
MERGE on Sales.Orders carries known concurrency and edge-case hazards; prefer separate UPDATE/INSERT logic.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments writes unchanged values, generating unnecessary locks and transaction log activity.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 filters on a broad non-key attribute rather than a key.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' blocks a SQL Server worker thread synchronously.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is executed outside a TRY...CATCH block, risking orphaned open transactions on error.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON overrides automatic identity generation and couples code to explicit key management.
EXEC sp_who omits the sys. schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 modifies session row-limiting behavior for all subsequent statements and is never reset to 0.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (...) omits an explicit target column list.
The literal CategoryID value 99 is hard-coded directly in the INSERT VALUES clause.
INSERT INTO #DemoCustomers omits an explicit target column list.
LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' starts with a leading wildcard, preventing an index seek on UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
User-supplied parameter @CustomerName is concatenated directly into @sql without escaping or parameterization, creating a SQL injection vulnerability.
EXEC sp_executesql omits the sys. schema qualifier.
sp_executesql @sql executes dynamic SQL without passing @CustomerName as a strongly typed parameter.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers has no WHERE clause and overwrites CustomerCategoryID on every row in the table.
Filtering o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' in the WHERE clause eliminates NULL-extended rows from LEFT JOIN Sales.Orders, implicitly turning it into an INNER JOIN.
The date constant '2016-01-01' is hard-coded in the WHERE clause without a named variable or parameter.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN under ANSI_NULLS ON and returns no rows; use IS NULL.
Calling scalar UDF dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the SELECT list can force row-by-row execution across Sales.Customers.
The CATCH block handles errors from an explicit transaction without checking XACT_STATE() or issuing ROLLBACK TRANSACTION.
The CATCH block selects ERROR_MESSAGE() without rethrowing the error, masking failure from the caller.
WITH (INDEX = 1) hard-codes an index hint on Sales.Customers, preventing optimizer plan adaptation and risking failure if indexes change.
Query nests three levels of derived tables (t1, t2, t3) unnecessarily; flatten the query or refactor to a CTE.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' uses a leading wildcard, preventing an index seek on UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
SELECT * FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti(@CustomerName) retrieves all columns without an explicit column list.
Querying multi-statement table-valued function dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti prevents query inlining and degrades cardinality estimation compared to an inline TVF.
